title: Vendor value: Concentration forecasts face diverse competition
desc: Examines direct model use, lawyer-built tools and in-house demand while investment announcements fail to establish durable returns.

kps.k: The central dispute concerns who captures durable value from legal AI, not simply whether lawyers adopt it.
kps.d: The discussion contrasts specialist applications such as Harvey and Legora with general-purpose models, lawyer-built tools, established legal-information platforms and AI-first service providers. Abramowitz frames the strategic choice as moving beyond software purchases toward new workflows and business models. Much of the material consists of his introductions, investment opinions and interview agendas rather than guests’ developed arguments or comparative evidence.

qs.q: At the same time, the frontier model companies, OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, xAI, now SpaceX, and others are lurking in the background, constantly raising the question of how much value belongs in the application layer or the harness layer now versus the model layer.
qs.a: Is Building Your Own AI the New Path to Attention? — William (Will) Chen of Mike OSS on Legally Disrupted ep. 51 · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: But they're not spending enough time focusing on, what are we going to need to do as a business because AI exists in the world?
qs.a: E49 - Harvey and Legora vs AI First Firms, Logan Brown, Soxton · AI-native providers · 2026

kps.k: Direct model use and lawyer-built software challenge specialist vendors, but the excerpts do not establish equivalent performance or displacement.
kps.d: Abramowitz reports that Quinn Emanuel built litigation workflows on Claude and that Will Chen created a functioning open-source application layer in two weeks. He also reports Carolyn Elefant’s view that general-purpose models outperform some legal-specific products. These examples make build-versus-buy a concrete question, but the proposed order-of-magnitude productivity gain remains hypothetical. Abramowitz welcomes independent builders while explicitly disagreeing with Chen’s degree of criticism and retaining confidence in Harvey and Legora.

qs.q: For example, Quinn Emanuel built their own proprietary system (the "Kerch Bench") entirely on top of Claude.
qs.a: Is Harvey vs. Legora Turning into Harvey vs. Legora vs. Claude? · Market & press · 2026

qs.q: While most critics stop at tweeting or posting cringy safeposts on LinkedIn, Will actually used “vibe coding” tools to build a functioning application layer in just two weeks.
qs.a: Is Building Your Own AI the New Path to Attention? — William (Will) Chen of Mike OSS on Legally Disrupted ep. 51 · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

kps.k: Predictions of extreme concentration compete with accounts of a diverse market lacking demonstrated network effects.
kps.d: The Junestrand interview forecasts that a leader could capture 90% of the market and links that expectation to rapid execution; the supplied speaker markers do not clearly attribute the entire passage. Elsewhere, Abramowitz challenges the Harvey–Legora two-company narrative and argues that additional users do not currently improve either product’s core value. Centari’s deal-intelligence niche, incumbent platforms and foundation-model entry illustrate alternative competitive positions. None of these excerpts supplies market analysis establishing either winner-takes-all concentration or lasting fragmentation.

qs.q: Number one will grab 90% and number two to number 10 will share the remaining 10%.
qs.a: Legora CEO, Max Junestrand: $7M ARR in a Day | Harvey vs Legora: Is a Legal AI Winner Takes All? · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: Giving the impression that legal AI is perhaps a two-horse race, we challenged that narrative.
qs.a: E38 - How Will SaaSpocalypse Affect AI For Legal: Spellbook CEO Scott Stevenson · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

kps.k: Investment momentum and adoption announcements do not resolve questions about retention, revenue quality or venture returns.
kps.d: Reported acquisitions, valuations and fundraising underpin the growth narrative. Junestrand reports $7 million in ARR additions in one day in 2025, while Tromans forecasts near-universal major-firm adoption and saturation within roughly 18 months of his discussion. These are company claims and forecasts, not verified operating results. Abramowitz simultaneously warns that recurring revenue may depend on temporary innovation budgets and raises Robin AI’s reported layoffs and funding difficulties as an unresolved warning sign. His optimism about stronger founders and Sandstone accompanies a disclosed investment in Sandstone; it does not establish product effectiveness or future returns.

qs.q: >> In a single day in 2025, we added 7  million of AR in 24 hours.
qs.a: Legora CEO, Max Junestrand: $7M ARR in a Day | Harvey vs Legora: Is a Legal AI Winner Takes All? · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: Effectively, we're going to hit market saturation, TAM saturation, in I would guess, 18 months, if not sooner.
qs.a: E28 - Zach and Richard's Excellent Legal AI Adventure: Inside Eudia's Groundbreaking AI-First Law Firm · Market & press · 2025

kps.k: In-house legal departments emerge as an independent market, rather than merely following law firms’ technology choices.
kps.d: Abramowitz says in-house adoption has matched or sometimes exceeded law-firm adoption, although he supplies no comparative statistics. He distinguishes general-purpose tools, vendors serving both markets and products designed specifically for legal departments. His Sandstone thesis targets friction between legal teams and the business across document review and advice, not just contract analysis. The practical question is whether vendors solve buyer-side workflow problems and secure durable budgets; publicity around major law-firm rollouts does not establish where demand is strongest.

qs.q: One of the most surprising things to me is that the adoption of AI tools in-house has actually maintained pace, and in some instances, actually exceeded that of law firms.
qs.a: E35 - Are Legal AI Assistants Moving In-House? GC AI Founder Cecilia Ziniti · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: How can we give answers, not just on contracts, but on any document that needs to be reviewed back to the business without holding up the business, without making it move any slower?
qs.a: E36 - Too Much FOMO: Why I'm Back on the Legal AI Startup Investor Train with Sandstone CEO Nick Fleisher · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

kps.k: AI-first firms introduce a service-delivery challenge distinct from competition among software vendors.
kps.d: Abramowitz points to Eudia’s Arizona launch, Manifest OS’s corporate-immigration positioning and growing enquiries about joining AI-first firms. He argues that AI could reduce leading lawyers’ dependence on large-firm infrastructure and potentially disrupt incumbent ALSPs such as Axiom. He also offers an anecdotal procurement mechanism: service-provider arrangements can access outside-counsel budgets when technology budgets are constrained. These reports do not establish superior service economics, a broad departure trend or inevitable AmLaw entry. Separately, he rejects claims that Harvey and Legora plan to become law firms themselves.

qs.q: And one of the best examples I've been highlighting in recent years is firms need to be aware that once their top lawyers start using AI, they may come to the conclusion that, you know what, I don't necessarily need this big law firm anymore.
qs.a: E49 - Harvey and Legora vs AI First Firms, Logan Brown, Soxton · AI-native providers · 2026

qs.q: But now as some of these firms are growing both in the sheer number of them, the brand recognition and the scale, I'm hearing more lawyers asking should I be joining one of these firms.

kps.k: Infrastructure, integration and partnerships offer a competing account of specialist vendors’ value beyond model access.
kps.d: Harvey’s founders describe a shift from an individual assistant toward infrastructure integrating legal systems, memory and multi-step agentic workflows, while acknowledging security and ethical-wall challenges. Sean Fitzpatrick presents the LexisNexis–Harvey alliance as part of a personalised-assistant strategy combining work product, authoritative legal materials and task automation; both companies will also develop independently. Legora’s Chris Williams emphasises implementation partners, publishers and shared user learning. These are strategies and intended benefits, not measured proof of differentiation, efficiency or quality gains.

qs.q: With host Bob Ambrogi, they discuss Harvey’s vision for becoming an AI operating system that integrates across the entire legal tech ecosystem, their focus on memory and agentic AI that can handle complex multi-step workflows, and the massive infrastructure challenges of deploying AI at scale across global law firms while maintaining ethical walls and data security.
qs.a: LawNext: From Roommates to Billionaires — Harvey's Founders Gabriel Pereyra and Winston Weinberg on Building AI Infrastructure for Law · Market & press · 2026

qs.q: It's going to have access to higher work product, it's going to have access to our collection of, you know, one of the world's largest collections of authoritative legal materials.
qs.a: Ep 296: How LexisNexis and Harvey Are Partnering to Reshape Legal AI, with LexisNexis CEO Sean Fitzpatrick · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

kps.k: Assistance and autonomous workflow replacement require different standards of readiness.
kps.d: The Abramowitz–Tromans discussion anticipates both modes but treats fully automated workflows as currently inadequate. Tromans argues that unreliable delegation loses value when humans must redo the work and uses a hypothetical NDA process to show how automation could multiply errors. Katya Fisher reports useful targeted reporting and redlining but says complex private-equity negotiations still need humans. Abramowitz’s separate claim that lawyers exaggerate hallucination concerns creates a tension in emphasis, not a resolved empirical disagreement. The excerpts provide neither comparative accuracy tests nor measured verification costs.

qs.q: We're probably going to end up with both, but 99 percent of all the discourse around AI is around that AI is an assistant, and understandably because A, you don't want to scare the crap out of the bias, two, because fully automated workflows are not good enough yet.
qs.a: E27 - Zach and Richard's Legal AI Adventure: Big Deals and AI Revolution · Market & press · 2025

qs.q: But if you say something like, write me an NDA and it screws it up, because it's understanding of what you want is inaccurate, and you've automated that, you've handed that over, you've effectively created a weapon of mass destruction within your own business, because it's just pumping out wrong stuff.
qs.a: E37 -  Zach and Richard’s Excellent Legal AI Adventure: Claude and the Legaltech Apocalypse · Market & press · 2026

kps.k: The proposed organisational response combines experimentation, skill development and business redesign rather than purchasing alone.
kps.d: Abramowitz recommends startup partnerships and argues that their greater potential lies in enabling unfamiliar ways of working, not only accelerating existing tasks. He distinguishes routine AI use from a deeper AI mindset and disputes an unnamed lawyer’s belief that this mindset cannot be taught, relying on his coaching experience. Career-transition anecdotes and Logan Brown’s expectation of less anxiety-inducing legal work suggest possible benefits for lawyers, but do not establish net employment gains or improved working conditions. The practical implications remain strategic proposals rather than validated implementation guidance.

qs.q: One of the things that I've done over the last many years since starting my consulting company, is I felt that if I was out telling legal firms and legal departments why they needed to partner with startups and why that was important part of future proofing, then I should drink that Kool-Aid myself.
qs.a: E26 - Exploring Legal Tech Investments in the Post-ChatGPT World with Chris Fisher and Jonathan Levy · Market & press · 2025

qs.q: And if I'm thinking about where early stage companies could be really valuable to law firms moving forward, it's in helping them see the 2.0, helping them see like, hey, this is what it can really be.
qs.a: How BigLaw Can and Should Partner with Early-Stage Startups · Law firms · 2025

vlens.an: This curated source from the regulators, courts and professional-bodies voice does not engage the cluster’s principal dispute over which legal-AI vendors or delivery models will capture durable value, whether competition will concentrate, or whether investment and adoption will produce lasting returns. Instead, Abramowitz redirects the inquiry toward profession-wide adoption, courtroom misuse and the unequal acceptance of AI across institutional roles. His central concern is that lawyers strongly support AI for their own research and analytics while being much less willing to accept AI-assisted decision-making by judges or arbitrators; he also alleges a regulatory double standard, although the supplied excerpt does not develop that claim. This focus may affect the conditions under which vendors operate, but it offers no analysis of vendor differentiation, market structure, retention, revenue quality or value capture. Because the evidence contains only Abramowitz’s introductory framing and no substantive remarks from the named guests, it does not support conclusions about internal variation within this professional voice.

qs.q: So according to multiple surveys from Wharton, Law 360, Thomson Reuters and the ACC, a bunch, AI usage in the legal profession flipped from a minority to a clear majority.
qs.a: E46 - AI for Judges? AAA CEO Bridget McCormack and Learned Hand CEO Shlomo Klapper · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: Nearly 90% of lawyers were deeply supportive of AI in their own research and analytics, but that support drops to 23% when it comes to either a judge or an arbitrator using AI to make a decision.
qs.a: E46 - AI for Judges? AAA CEO Bridget McCormack and Learned Hand CEO Shlomo Klapper · Regulators & courts · 2026

vlens.an: The AI-native legal-provider voice accepts the cluster’s principal proposition that durable legal-AI value will be contested across multiple models rather than captured automatically by a small group of software vendors. It materially develops that proposition by identifying AI-first legal-service providers as a separate competitive channel: AI may reduce lawyers’ dependence on large-firm infrastructure, enable new career destinations, challenge incumbent ALSPs, and let technology-enabled services draw on outside-counsel budgets that may be more accessible than legal departments’ technology budgets. The common reasoning is therefore business-model and procurement based, not merely about model performance or software adoption. Material variation lies in emphasis: some excerpts stress lawyer mobility and competitive pressure on traditional firms; another proposes a budget-access advantage; another raises disruption of incumbent ALSPs; and Logan Brown anticipates better-quality legal work as undesirable tasks recede. The evidentiary basis remains limited: much of it is Abramowitz’s introductory framing, anecdotal enquiries, reported fundraising and forward-looking hypotheses rather than guests’ developed arguments, comparative operating data or proof of durable economics. Accordingly, these curated sources extend the proposition with concrete mechanisms but do not establish broad migration, superior returns, actual ALSP displacement or inevitable AmLaw entry.

qs.q: And one of the best examples I've been highlighting in recent years is firms need to be aware that once their top lawyers start using AI, they may come to the conclusion that, you know what, I don't necessarily need this big law firm anymore.
qs.a: E49 - Harvey and Legora vs AI First Firms, Logan Brown, Soxton · AI-native providers · 2026

qs.q: You know,  very often legal departments don't necessarily have a big tech budget, but they do have an outside counsel budget.
qs.a: Dan Mishin — Manifest OS: an AI-first corporate-immigration firm built as software plus a lawyer network · AI-native providers · 2026

vlens.an: These selected traditional-practice sources accept the synthesis’s core proposition that durable legal-AI value is contested among specialist vendors, general-purpose models, lawyer-built products and organisational capabilities. They materially extend it by identifying two concrete law-firm responses beyond purchasing specialist software: developing products inside practising firms and partnering with early-stage companies to redesign work rather than merely accelerate existing workflows. They also argue that effective adoption requires a cultivable AI mindset, although this addresses organisational readiness more than competitive structure. Material internal variation concerns where value may accrue: one source predicts that improving general-purpose models could outpace legal-specific products; another presents a practice-embedded specialist product as gaining traction; and a third sees startups’ larger opportunity in enabling unfamiliar “2.0” workflows. These are compatible possibilities rather than a settled market forecast. The evidence remains largely anecdotal, introductory or predictive: it does not establish comparative model performance, named-customer adoption, durable revenue, displacement of specialist vendors or realised returns. Because the corpus is curated, these positions should not be treated as representative of traditional law firms generally.

qs.q: She had a great post recently about how she thinks some of the basic models like ChatGPT, Clawd, Google Gemini are actually getting to be much better than some of the legal specific tools, even at legal specific tasks.

vlens.an: Within this curated selection, the legal-tech-vendor voice broadly supports the proposition that durable legal-AI value capture remains unsettled amid diverse competition. Common reasons include competition from frontier models and lawyer-built tools; specialist niches such as deal intelligence and in-house workflows; established platforms combining authoritative content with automation; and differentiation strategies based on integration, implementation partners and user communities. The sources repeatedly distinguish adoption, funding, valuations and company-reported growth from evidence of retention, revenue quality, market share or durable returns. Material internal variation remains: Legora’s winner-takes-all forecast directly opposes the diverse-market framing; LegalQuants redirects attention toward people-led value; Ivo and LexisNexis build on the proposition with concrete accounts of technology transition and content-plus-workflow differentiation; and career, fundraising and general-adoption excerpts are unclear on value capture. Some vendor-aligned sources are also more bullish about Harvey, Legora, Sandstone or niche providers than the synthesis, but their claims are generally predictions, strategies or qualitative impressions rather than demonstrated outcomes. This characterises only the supplied curated sources, not legal-tech vendors generally.

vlens.an: The curated market-analyst, consultancy and press sources support the proposition that legal-AI adoption does not by itself determine who will capture durable value. Their common reasoning is that specialist vendors such as Harvey and Legora face several distinct forms of competition: direct use of frontier models, lawyer-built workflows, incumbent legal-information platforms, niche applications and AI-first service providers. They also repeatedly separate funding, valuations, deals and customer announcements from evidence of retention, revenue quality, product differentiation or venture returns. Several sources further question winner-takes-all dynamics because wider adoption does not currently appear to improve the core product through network effects. Material internal variation remains. Some sources report rapid Harvey growth, stronger founder talent and likely near-universal adoption among major firms, while Harvey’s infrastructure, integration and agentic-workflow strategy offers a substantive account of why specialist vendors might retain value beyond model access. Others stress foundation-model pressure, unreliable autonomous workflows, temporary innovation budgets and company-level funding difficulties. These are mostly forecasts, reported claims, hypotheticals and introductory commentary rather than comparative performance or financial evidence. Some excerpts address only investment activity, professional background or interview framing and are therefore individually unclear, but they do not create a substantive counter-position. Because this is a curated set, this assessment characterises only the supplied sources and does not imply that it represents market analysts, consultancies or the press generally.

qs.q: Harvey as a software and Legora as a software, any of these products, I don't see any way right now in which they become more valuable based on how many people that use them.

qs.q: You've got customers that aren't really customers, revenue that's technically recurring, but only until next year's innovation budget disappears, and the constant looming threat of getting steamrolled by open AI.
qs.a: E23 - Investment Hype vs. Reality in Legal AI, Eli Amsellem, Ridge Ventures · Market & press · 2025

elens.an:
The 2025 sources broadly support the proposition that rising legal-AI adoption and investment activity do not determine who will capture durable value. Their common reasoning is that headline valuations, funding rounds, acquisitions and reported client growth are weaker evidence than retention, revenue quality, workflow fit and defensible differentiation. They also depict competition as structurally diverse: specialist vendors face general-purpose models, established legal-information platforms, niche applications and AI-first service providers. Several sources further distinguish useful assistant functions from autonomous workflow replacement, judging the latter insufficiently reliable for complex work.

Material variation concerns where defensible value might arise. Some sources stress commoditisation and the risk that foundation-model providers overtake specialist tools. Others identify possible specialist advantages in authoritative content, workflow integration, implementation partnerships, user communities or narrow deal-specific applications. Two sources materially extend the proposition: Fitzpatrick specifies how personalised automation combined with authoritative legal materials could differentiate the LexisNexis–Harvey alliance, while the startup-partnership discussion proposes a shift from accelerating existing work to enabling new workflows. More bullish material forecasts rapid major-firm adoption and market saturation, and Harvey’s reported growth illustrates commercial momentum, but these sources still do not establish lasting concentration or returns. Several introductory excerpts are too undeveloped to resolve the proposition at all. Overall, the evidence supports the synthesis’s caution rather than either a winner-takes-all forecast or a firm prediction of lasting fragmentation. Because the corpus is curated, these relationships should not be read as measuring how prevalent any view was in 2025.

qs.q: You've got customers that aren't really customers, revenue that's technically recurring, but only until next year's innovation budget disappears, and the constant looming threat of getting steamrolled by open AI.

elens.an: The curated 2026 sources overall support the proposition that durable legal-AI value remains contested rather than settled by adoption, fundraising or headline valuations. Common reasons include competition from direct foundation-model use, lawyer-built and open-source tools, established platforms, specialist vendors, in-house-focused products and AI-first service providers; the apparent absence of current adoption-driven network effects; and the lack of verified evidence on retention, revenue quality, comparative performance or venture returns. Several sources materially elaborate where value might nevertheless accrue—through workflow integration, authoritative content, security, agentic infrastructure, buyer-side problem solving or access to outside-counsel budgets—but mostly present these as strategies, anecdotes or forecasts rather than demonstrated advantages. Internal variation is significant: one source predicts a winner-takes-all market in which the leader captures 90%, while others challenge a Harvey–Legora duopoly; some remain bullish on specialist vendors despite lawyer-built alternatives; and some redirect attention to people, careers, adoption or adjudication rather than vendor economics. These divergent claims make the market outcome genuinely disputed, but do not overturn the period’s overall alignment with the proposition’s cautious, diverse-competition framing. Because the corpus is curated, this assessment characterises only the supplied sources and does not imply prevalence across broader stakeholder groups.
